metadata.title: O'CONNOR v. Consolidated Coin Caterers Corp., 517 U.S. 308 (1996) (No. 95-354)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: O'CONNOR v. Consolidated Coin Caterers Corp.

Opinion filed: 1996-04-01

Docket No.: 95-354

Citations:
• 134 L. Ed. 2d 433
• 116 S. Ct. 1307
• 517 U.S. 308
• 1996 U.S. LEXIS 2168

Case holding summaries:
• inference of discrimination cannot be drawn from the replacement of one worker with another insignificantly younger
• holding in an ADEA case that "[t]he fact that one person in the protected class has lost out to another person in the protected class is . . . irrelevant, so long as he has lost out because of his age. "
• fact that one person in the ADEA protected class has lost out to another person in the protected class is not determinative as long as the person lost out because of his age
• recognizing that the ADEA "limits the protected class to those who are 40 or older"
• discussing proof of age discrimination
• leaving open the question of whether McDonnell Douglas applies in ADEA cases
• inference of age discrimination exists when 56 year old plaintiff replaced by 40 year old
• “In the age-discrimination context, such an inference [that an employment decision was based on an illegal criterion] cannot be drawn from the replacement of one worker with another worker insignificantly younger.”
• explaining that an inference of age bias "cannot be drawn from the replacement of one worker with another worker insignificantly younger"
• assuming that the McDonnell Douglas framework applies to ADEA claims
• modifying the fourth prong of the ADEA prima facie case
• 56-year-old worker may challenge under ADEA discharge and replacement by a 40-year-old worker
• applying Hicks analysis in summary judgment context
• explaining that replacement by someone “substantially younger” can be an indicator of age discrimination
• noting “the fact that a replacement is substantially younger than the plaintiff is a far more reliable indicator of age discrimination”
• addressing the fourth element of the prima facie case under the ADEA
• replacement of plaintiff by person in protected age class but substantially younger permits inference of age discrimination, but no inference drawn from replacement by one insignificantly younger
• outlining elements of prima facie case for claim of race discrimination under Title VII and age discrimination under ADEA
• holding that "[b]ecause it lacks probative value, the fact that an ADEA plaintiff was replaced by someone outside the protected class is not a proper element of the McDonnell Douglas prima facie case"
• holding that a prima facie case cannot be established if the plaintiff's replacement is "insignificantly younger" than the plaintiff
• discussing elements of prima facie case
• a prima facie case could possibly be based on the "very thin evidence" of a 68 year-old being replaced by a 65 year-old
• assuming that the McDonnell Douglas framework applies in the ADEA context
• "[T]he fact that a replacement is substantially younger than the plaintiff is a far more reliable indicator of age discrimination than is the fact that the plaintiff was replaced by someone outside the protected class."
• holding that a plaintiff need not be replaced by someone outside the protected class to maintain a claim under the ADEA
• leaving the question of the applicability of the McDonnell Douglas paradigm in ADEA cases open
• assuming arguendo that McDonnell Douglas applies under ADEA
• stating "irrelevant factor[s]" should not take precedence over "evidence adequate to create an inference that an employment decision was based on a[n] 36 [illegal] discriminatory criterion"
• holding that "[b]ecause it lacks probative value, the fact that an ADEA plaintiff was replaced by someone outside the protected class is not a proper element of the McDonnell Douglas prima facie case"
• holding that, under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, an age discrimination plaintiff is not required to show that he was replaced by someone outside the protected class
• prima facie case requires evidence adequate to create inference of discrimination, which cannot be drawn from the replacement of one worker with another worker insignificantly younger
• plaintiff need not show he was replaced by a worker outside the protected class to make out a prima facie case of age discrimination
• no inference of age discrimination can be drawn from the replacement of one worker with another worker insignificantly younger
• "In the age-discrimination context, such an inference [that an employment decision was based on age] cannot be drawn from the replacement of one worker with another worker insignificantly younger."
• noting that the ADEA "limits the protected class to those who are 40 or older"
• “As the very name ‘prima facie case’ suggests, there must be at least a logical connection between each element of the prima facie case and the illegal discrimination for which it establishes a legally mandatory, rebuttable presumption.”
• "In the age-discrimination context, such an inference [that an employment decision was based on an illegal criterion] cannot be drawn from the replacement of one worker with another worker insignificantly younger."
• holding that age discrimination plaintiff need not show that his replacement was outside the protected class
• "The fact that a replacement is substantially younger than the plaintiff is a far more reliable indicator of age discrimination than is the fact that the plaintiff was replaced by someone outside the protected class."
• "[S]uch an inference cannot be drawn from the replacement of one worker with another worker insignificantly younger."
• “In the age-discrimination context, such an inference [of discrimination] cannot be drawn from the replacement of one worker with another worker insignificantly younger.”
• modifying the fourth element of the scheme
• finding that the "fact that a [selectee] is substantially younger than the plaintiff is a far more reliable indicator of age discrimination than is the fact that the plaintiff was replaced by someone outside the protected class."
• assuming the application of the Title VII evidentiary framework set forth in McDonnell Douglas to the ADEA context is correct
• modifying the fourth prong of the scheme
• "In the age discrimination context . . . an inference [of discriminatory intent] cannot be drawn from the replacement of one worker with another worker insignificantly younger."
• holding that a plaintiff need not be replaced by someone outside the protected class to maintain a claim under the ADEA
• assuming arguendo that McDonnell Douglas applies under ADEA
• stating "irrelevant factor[s]" should not take precedence over "evidence adequate to create an inference that an employment decision was based on a[n] [illegal] discriminatory criterion"
• where the Fourth Circuit's requirement to show replacement by a worker under 40 was rejected
